strengths: The method addresses a useful computer vision problem: spatial question answering directly from monocular RGB video without sensor depth or prebuilt maps at inference. Using CUT3R’s latent geometry and camera tokens avoids a separate point-cloud encoding pipeline.

The reported VSI-Bench results are strong: 60.90 overall versus 57.74 for the data-finetuned baseline (Table 3). Improvements in absolute distance (43.67 to 49.38), relative direction (68.93 to 80.52), and route planning (40.72 to 45.36) support the usefulness of adding geometric features.

The automated supervision pipeline is a potentially valuable contribution. It repurposes existing scene annotations into 207,779 spatial QA pairs, including simulator-derived route questions, and introduces camera-centric evaluation tasks with 132,568 training and 6,042 test examples.

The component ablations provide evidence beyond comparisons against untuned models: removing camera or geometry tokens reduces overall performance. The appendix also supplies useful architectural dimensions, optimization settings, and data-generation rules.
weaknesses: The evaluation’s independence is insufficiently documented. Training data are generated from ScanNet, ScanNet++, and ARKitScenes, but the manuscript does not explain how VSI-Bench evaluation scenes are excluded. For VSTemporalI-Bench, Tables 5–6 report QA counts without stating whether scenes or videos are disjoint across training and testing. This does not establish leakage, but leaves a consequential uncertainty about whether the results demonstrate generalization to unseen environments.

The backbone configuration is inconsistent in a way that affects the central controlled comparison. Appendix A.2 specifies initialization from LLaVA-Video-7B-Qwen2, whereas the main text and Table 3 identify the finetuned baseline as LLaVA-NeXT-Video. These are different model identities; the manuscript does not establish that the full model and baseline share the same initialization. Consequently, the reported 3.16-point gain cannot confidently be attributed entirely to geometry fusion.

The VSTemporalI-Bench experiment lacks the controls needed to support its architectural claims. VLM-3R is explicitly finetuned on the benchmark’s training split, but equivalent training is not reported for competitors, and neither a data-matched visual-only baseline nor camera/geometry ablations are provided on this benchmark. The 58.8 score demonstrates performance of the complete trained system, but does not isolate the contribution of reconstruction features to temporal reasoning.

The temporal contribution is narrower than several claims suggest. All scenes are static, three of the five tasks concern individual frames, and the two sequence tasks derive answers from camera displacement. The paper acknowledges the static-scene restriction, but claims about dynamic environments and disentangling object motion from camera motion exceed the demonstrated evidence. Automated label quality is also not audited; for example, camera–object distance uses bounding-box surfaces rather than actual object surfaces.

The architectural novelty is primarily the integration of an existing frozen reconstruction model with standard cross-attention and instruction tuning. This can still be useful, but makes reliable attribution and dataset validation especially important. Scalability claims additionally lack inference latency or memory measurements. Overall, the practical merits are worthwhile, but uncertainty about evaluation separation and backbone matching, together with the uncontrolled temporal comparison, currently outweigh the evidence for acceptance.

strengths: VLM-3R addresses a useful computer vision problem: spatial question answering directly from monocular video. Integrating frozen CUT3R geometry and camera tokens with visual features is technically plausible and avoids requiring sensor depth or prebuilt maps at inference.

The reported VSI-Bench results are promising. Table 3 includes a data-matched fine-tuned baseline: the full model improves the average from 57.74 to 60.90, with substantial gains in absolute distance (43.67 to 49.38) and relative direction (68.93 to 80.52). These results provide evidence of value beyond instruction tuning alone.

The automated curation pipeline produces 207,779 spatial QA examples, including simulator-generated route questions. VSTemporalI-Bench adds potentially useful evaluation of camera displacement, movement direction, and viewpoint-dependent spatial relationships.

The supplementary material provides useful architectural dimensions, optimization settings, QA-generation rules, and task distributions. The paper also explicitly acknowledges that its temporal benchmark contains static scenes.
weaknesses: The evaluation's independence is insufficiently documented. Training data are generated from ScanNet, ScanNet++, and ARKitScenes, but the manuscript does not identify scene-level exclusions relative to VSI-Bench. For VSTemporalI-Bench, Tables 5–6 give QA counts without specifying whether splitting occurs by question, video, or scene. Because many questions can share the same underlying geometry, these omissions prevent assessing generalization to unseen environments. This is not evidence of leakage, but it is a material uncertainty affecting both principal evaluations.

The backbone description creates an important ambiguity in the controlled comparison. Appendix A.2 specifies initialization from LLaVA-Video-7B-Qwen2, whereas Table 3 identifies the fine-tuned baseline as LLaVA-NeXT-Video. The manuscript does not establish that both use identical initialization and input processing. Consequently, the otherwise valuable 3.16-point ablation gain cannot be confidently attributed entirely to the proposed spatial integration.

The temporal evaluation lacks the central matched-training control. Section 5.2 explicitly fine-tunes VLM-3R on VSTemporalI-Bench, but Table 2 provides neither an equivalently fine-tuned visual-only baseline nor geometry/camera-token ablations. Its 58.8 versus 44.0 comparison therefore does not isolate the contribution of geometry to temporal reasoning from task-specific supervision.

The contribution is primarily a useful integration of pretrained CUT3R features, standard cross-attention, and generated instruction data. Table 3 indicates that instruction tuning accounts for much of the headline improvement. There is no comparison against simpler geometry-integration alternatives to establish the particular value of the proposed fusion design.

Several claims exceed the demonstrated scope. Three of the five new benchmark tasks are frame-level, and all scenes are static, so the results support camera-motion and viewpoint reasoning rather than independently moving-object understanding. Scalability and time-sensitive applicability are asserted without inference latency or memory measurements. These are claim-calibration issues; the more consequential reasons for weak rejection are the unresolved evaluation independence and baseline comparability.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: spatial reasoning directly from monocular video. Integrating CUT3R’s latent geometry and camera tokens with appearance features is a technically plausible way to exploit pretrained reconstruction without requiring depth sensors or explicit maps at inference.

The reported VSI-Bench results are strong: 60.9 overall versus 45.4 for Gemini-1.5 Pro. More meaningfully, Table 3 reports an improvement over the data-finetuned baseline from 57.74 to 60.90, including gains in absolute distance, relative direction, and route planning.

The component ablations provide supporting evidence for the fusion design: removing camera or geometry tokens reduces the overall score to 59.09 or 59.46, respectively. The paper also acknowledges tasks where geometry provides little benefit.

The automated annotation pipeline and additional camera-motion tasks could be useful resources. The supplement supplies task-generation logic, dataset counts, fusion dimensions, and substantial training hyperparameter detail.
weaknesses: The principal concern is evaluation independence. Training data and evaluation resources draw on ScanNet, ScanNet++, and ARKitScenes, but the manuscript does not specify scene-level separation or exclusion of VSI-Bench evaluation scenes. For VSTemporalI-Bench, Tables 5–6 provide QA counts without explaining how scenes or videos are partitioned. This does not establish leakage, but leaves unseen-scene generalization—the basis of the main performance claims—unverified.

The identity of the matched baseline is unclear. The main text and Table 3 name LLaVA-NeXT-Video, whereas Appendix A.2 specifies initialization from LLaVA-Video-7B-Qwen2. These are distinct checkpoints. Without establishing that the full model and the no-geometry baseline use identical initialization and training, the reported 3.16-point architectural improvement cannot be cleanly attributed to the proposed fusion.

The temporal benchmark lacks an equally finetuned appearance-only baseline and camera/geometry ablations. VLM-3R is explicitly trained on its 132,568 training questions, while equivalent adaptation is not reported for the comparison models. Table 2 therefore demonstrates task-specific performance, but does not isolate the benefit of reconstruction features for temporal reasoning.

The temporal contribution is narrower than some claims suggest. All scenes are static, and three of the five tasks concern relationships at a single specified frame. The benchmark supports camera-motion and viewpoint-conditioned spatial understanding, but does not demonstrate independently moving-object reasoning or general dynamic-scene understanding.

The architecture primarily combines an existing reconstruction encoder, an existing VLM, and standard cross-attention. Its practical value can justify this incremental novelty, but the strongest evidence must consequently come from controlled experiments and reliable dataset construction. Those are precisely where the split and baseline ambiguities remain consequential.

Scalability and time-sensitive applicability are asserted without inference latency, memory, or video-length scaling measurements. Reproduction also requires clearer frame-sampling and evaluation protocols. These are secondary limitations; the recommendation primarily reflects uncertainty about evaluation independence and controlled attribution, despite the promising results and useful engineering contribution.

strengths: The paper addresses a useful computer-vision problem: spatial reasoning from monocular video without depth or prebuilt maps at inference. Combining CUT3R’s recurrent geometry and camera tokens with visual features is technically plausible, and the fusion equations clearly describe the core mechanism.

The spatial instruction dataset is a substantial contribution: 207,779 QA pairs, including 4,225 simulator-generated route-planning examples. The supplement provides task distributions, generation logic, and navigation templates, while the manuscript explicitly states that source-dataset train/test splits are respected.

Tables 1 and 6 include valuable data-matched comparisons. The full model scores 60.90 on VSI-Bench versus 57.74 for the reported fine-tuned baseline, with improvements in absolute distance, relative direction, and route planning. Removing either token type or replacing geometry fusion with 2D–2D fusion reduces performance.

Evaluation extends beyond the primary benchmark. Reported results include 101.9 CIDEr on ScanQA, 60.7 exact match on SQA3D, and an OST-Bench overall improvement from 39.3 to 42.9. The paper also measures general-capability tradeoffs and shows that mixing general video data improves Video-MME from 59.9 to 62.1.

The combination of useful training data, a camera-centric benchmark, and reported architectural gains provides substantive merit. These strengths place the paper near the acceptance boundary despite the experimental ambiguities below.
weaknesses: The identity of the base model is materially inconsistent. The main experiments and ablations identify LLaVA-NeXT-Video-7B, whereas Supplement A.2 explicitly initializes from LLaVA-Video-7B-Qwen2 with a SigLIP vision tower; Table 7 also uses LLaVA-Video-7B as the base. These are distinct checkpoints. Consequently, the manuscript does not establish that its central architecture-versus-baseline comparisons truly control for initialization.

The VSTI-Bench training protocol is insufficiently specified. The supplement lists 132,568 training and 6,042 test questions, but the experimental description does not clearly establish whether or how the temporal training split is used for Table 2. That table lacks a baseline fine-tuned on the same data, and token ablations are confined to VSI-Bench. The 58.8 result therefore does not isolate the proposed view tokens’ contribution to temporal reasoning.

The benchmark’s temporal interpretation is broader than its demonstrated coverage. Three of five tasks concern spatial relationships at a single specified frame; only camera displacement and movement direction explicitly require multiple frames. Static scenes are appropriately acknowledged, but no single-frame or endpoint-only control establishes how much sequence reasoning the overall score measures. Scene counts and human-evaluation procedures are also missing, limiting interpretation of benchmark diversity and the reported human score.

Architectural originality is incremental relative to the geometry-token VLMs discussed in the paper: the main changes are the CUT3R encoder and camera-token inclusion through standard residual cross-attention. Table D supports CUT3R’s overall advantage over VGGT, but does not isolate metric scale from recurrence or other encoder differences. In particular, VGGT slightly exceeds CUT3R on absolute distance and object size, so the proposed metric-scale explanation is only partially supported.

Several reporting errors overstate the evidence. Section 5.3 reports 50.09 without view tokens, whereas Table 6 gives 59.09, substantially changing the apparent effect size. Table 7 claims improvement across all categories despite counting falling from 63.1 to 49.6. The VSI discussion also combines baseline numbers from different models. These are correctable presentation issues, but they require careful auditing.

Broad generalization claims should be narrower. OpenEQA spatial performance improves from 49.95 to 51.60, but overall performance falls from 62.4 to 61.7; VQAv2 also decreases. ScanQA and SQA3D involve task-specific training rather than zero-shot transfer. Together with the unresolved checkpoint and temporal-training conditions, these limitations prevent a confident acceptance recommendation despite the promising results.

strengths: The problem is relevant: improving spatial reasoning from monocular video without requiring depth or preconstructed maps at inference. Combining CUT3R’s recurrent geometry and camera tokens with visual features is technically plausible, and the fusion equations are clearly specified.

The reported VSI-Bench results provide meaningful evidence beyond comparisons with untuned models. VLM-3R achieves 60.90 versus 57.74 for the reported fine-tuned baseline. Table 6 includes spatial-token, view-token, 2D–2D fusion, and explicit-point controls, with the full model performing best.

The data contribution has potential practical value: 207,779 spatial QA pairs, including 4,225 route-planning examples, plus a temporal dataset with 132,568 training and 6,042 test questions. The supplement describes metadata construction, task generation, and route templates, and the paper explicitly states that source-dataset train/test splits are respected.

Evaluation extends beyond the authors’ benchmark. Reported results include 101.9 CIDEr on ScanQA, 60.7 exact match on SQA3D, and an OST-Bench improvement from 39.3 to 42.9. The paper also measures general-capability degradation and shows that general-video data mixing recovers much of the Video-MME loss.
weaknesses: The base-model identity is materially inconsistent, compromising interpretation of the central comparisons. Tables 1 and 6 identify LLaVA-NeXT-Video as the fine-tuned baseline, whereas Appendix A.2 explicitly initializes VLM-3R from LLaVA-Video-7B-Qwen2 with a SigLIP vision tower; Table 7 also names LLaVA-Video as its base. These are different checkpoints, not interchangeable names. The manuscript does not establish whether the reported 3.2-point architectural gain uses an otherwise identical backbone and training setup. This is a principal reason for the weak-reject recommendation.

The temporal contribution lacks a decisive controlled evaluation. Table 2 omits a baseline fine-tuned on the same data and provides no spatial-token or view-token ablations on VSTI-Bench. Moreover, although the supplement defines a 132,568-question temporal training split, the training descriptions emphasize the 200K spatial dataset without clearly specifying whether or how temporal training data enter the reported models. Consequently, the 58.8 score cannot establish that camera-token fusion, rather than task-specific supervision, explains the temporal improvement.

The metric-scale explanation is stronger than the evidence. Table D supports CUT3R as the better overall encoder, but VGGT slightly exceeds it on absolute distance (49.8 versus 49.4) and object size (70.8 versus 69.2); CUT3R’s clearest measurement advantage is room size. Replacing VGGT with CUT3R changes temporal processing and other architectural properties as well as scale priors. Without a scale-specific control or geometry-error analysis, the results establish an encoder preference rather than isolating metric scale as the cause.

VSTI-Bench is useful but narrower than some temporal-understanding claims suggest. Three of its five tasks are explicitly frame-level; the other two concern camera displacement and direction in static scenes. Appendix B.2 acknowledges this scope, but there is no single-frame or frame-order control showing how much performance requires temporal integration. The manuscript also does not document the human-evaluation sample size and procedure underlying the 77.0 human score, or quantify automated-label quality.

Originality is primarily in system integration and data curation. The manuscript itself describes prior geometry-augmented VLMs that fuse reconstruction features with language models. The proposed attention and residual fusion are standard, while CUT3R supplies the geometric representation. This can still be a useful contribution, but it makes reliable matched comparisons and attribution particularly important; the reporting ambiguities above weaken that case.

Several correctable reporting problems overstate the evidence. Section 5.3 gives 50.09 without view tokens, while Table 6 reports 59.09. Table 7 claims improvement across all categories despite counting declining from 63.1 to 49.6 and Agent Info declining slightly. OpenEQA overall performance also falls from 62.4 to 61.7. These issues are secondary to the experimental-control concerns, but they require more restrained claims about robustness and preservation of general capabilities.

strengths: The method addresses a useful computer-vision problem: spatial reasoning from monocular video without depth or prebuilt maps at inference. Combining CUT3R geometry and camera tokens with visual features through residual cross-attention is technically coherent.

The reported VSI-Bench improvements extend beyond additional training data. Tables 1 and 6 show 60.90 versus 57.74 for the spatially fine-tuned baseline, with particularly substantial gains in relative direction and absolute distance. Removing either geometry or view tokens reduces performance, and explicit-point and 2D-only fusion alternatives perform worse.

The data contribution is substantial: 207,779 spatial QA pairs, including 4,225 route-planning examples, and a camera-aware benchmark with 132,568 training and 6,042 test questions. The supplement explains task-generation rules, and the manuscript explicitly states adherence to source-dataset splits.

Evaluation is reasonably broad. Results include 101.9 CIDEr on ScanQA, 60.7 exact match on SQA3D, and an OST-Bench improvement from 39.3 to 42.9. General-purpose evaluations also expose specialization costs rather than reporting only favorable spatial results.
weaknesses: A material inconsistency concerns the backbone underlying the comparisons. Tables 1 and 6 identify LLaVA-NeXT-Video as the fine-tuned baseline, whereas Appendix A.2 explicitly initializes VLM-3R from LLaVA-Video-7B-Qwen2 with SigLIP; Table 7 also identifies LLaVA-Video as its base. Without a consistent checkpoint specification, the central 3.2-point gain cannot be confidently attributed entirely to geometry fusion rather than backbone differences.

The VSTI-Bench training protocol is unclear. The supplement provides a 132,568-example training split, but the experimental description does not clearly establish whether or how this split is used for Table 2. That table lacks a comparably fine-tuned baseline, and the view-token ablation is conducted only on VSI-Bench. Consequently, the 58.8 temporal-benchmark score does not isolate the contribution of camera tokens from task-specific supervision.

Architectural originality is incremental relative to the acknowledged geometry-augmented VLMs: the main changes are CUT3R, camera tokens, and conventional cross-attention. Table D supports the encoder choice overall, but does not isolate metric scale as the cause: VGGT slightly outperforms CUT3R on absolute distance and object size. The strongest evidence supports the combined system rather than the specific causal explanation about metric-scale representations.

The new benchmark has a narrower scope than some temporal-reasoning claims suggest. Three of its five tasks are explicitly frame-level, and all scenes are static. Camera displacement and direction are valuable additions, but aggregate performance does not establish reasoning about independently moving objects. Scene counts, annotation-quality audits, and the human-evaluation protocol are also insufficiently documented to assess benchmark diversity and reliability.

Several reporting issues require correction: the view-token ablation is 59.09 in Table 6 but 50.09 in the text; Table 7 claims improvement across all categories despite counting falling from 63.1 to 49.6. Broader transfer is mixed, including OpenEQA overall performance decreasing from 62.4 to 61.7. These are secondary to the backbone and training-protocol ambiguities. Overall, the useful system and data contributions place the paper near acceptance, but the unresolved provenance of its central comparisons makes the current recommendation borderline.
